questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to calculate the Laplace transform 

$$
L{t\operatorname{cosh}⁡7t}.
$$

 
Select the correct options in the reasoning below. You may make use of the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\,s>\omega .
$$

Let $f(t)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡7t$ and $L{f(t)}=F(s).$ By the smoothness property of Laplace transforms,

$$
L{tf(t)}={{field-1}}.
$$

The Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={{field-2}},\,s>7.
$$

We have that

$$
{F}^{′}(s)={{field-3}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
L{t\operatorname{cosh}⁡7t}={{field-4}},\,s>7.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for every real $s>a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence. Moreover, for each integer $n\ge 0$ and every such $s,$ we have

$$
L{{t}^{n}f(t)}=(-1)^{n}{F}^{(n)}(s).
$$

In particular, for $n=1,$ we have

$$
L{tf(t)}=-{F}^{′}(s).
$$

We have that $f(t)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡7t.$ Using the given result with $\omega =7,$ the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is 

$$
F(s)=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-49},\,s>7.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $s,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-49}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(s({s}^{2}-49)^{-1}) \\  & =({s}^{2}-49)^{-1}+s(-({s}^{2}-49)^{-2}\cdot 2s) \\  & =\frac{{s}^{2}-49}{({s}^{2}-49)^{2}}-\frac{2{s}^{2}}{({s}^{2}-49)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-49-{s}^{2}}{({s}^{2}-49)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+49}{({s}^{2}-49)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the smoothness property,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t\operatorname{cosh}⁡7t}=-{F}^{′}(s)=\frac{{s}^{2}+49}{({s}^{2}-49)^{2}},\,s>7.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to calculate the Laplace transform 

$$
L{{t}^{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(-6t)}.
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below. You may make use of the following results:

$$
L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\,s>\omega .
$$

Let $f(t)=\operatorname{sinh}⁡(-6t)$ and $F(s)=L{f(t)}.$ By the smoothness property of Laplace transforms, we have

$$
L{{t}^{2}f(t)}={{field-1}}.
$$

Using $\operatorname{sinh}⁡(-6t)=-\operatorname{sinh}⁡6t,$ the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={{field-2}},\,s>6.
$$

We have that

$$
{F}^{″}(s)={{field-3}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
L{{t}^{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(-6t)}={{field-4}},\,s>6.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for every real $s>a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence. Moreover, for each integer $n\ge 0$ and every such $s,$ we have

$$
L{{t}^{n}f(t)}=(-1)^{n}{F}^{(n)}(s).
$$

In particular, for $n=2,$ we have

$$
L{{t}^{2}f(t)}={F}^{″}(s).
$$

We have that

$$
f(t)=\operatorname{sinh}⁡(-6t)=-\operatorname{sinh}⁡6t.
$$

Using the given result with $\omega =6,$ the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sinh}⁡6t$ is $\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-36},$ so

$$
F(s)=-\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-36},\,s>6.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $s,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-36}) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(6({s}^{2}-36)^{-1}) \\  & =-(-6({s}^{2}-36)^{-2}\cdot 2s) \\  & =\frac{12s}{({s}^{2}-36)^{2}} \\ {F}^{″}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{12s}{({s}^{2}-36)^{2}}) \\  & =12\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{s}{({s}^{2}-36)^{2}}) \\  & =12\cdot (\frac{(s)^{′}\cdot ({s}^{2}-36)^{2}-s\cdot {(({s}^{2}-36)^{2})}^{′}}{({s}^{2}-36)^{4}}) \\  & =12\cdot (\frac{({s}^{2}-36)^{2}-s\cdot 2({s}^{2}-36)\cdot 2s}{({s}^{2}-36)^{4}}) \\  & =12\cdot (\frac{({s}^{2}-36)^{2}-4{s}^{2}({s}^{2}-36)}{({s}^{2}-36)^{4}}) \\  & =12\cdot (\frac{{s}^{2}-36-4{s}^{2}}{({s}^{2}-36)^{3}}) \\  & =12\cdot (\frac{-3{s}^{2}-36}{({s}^{2}-36)^{3}}) \\  & =-\frac{36{s}^{2}+432}{({s}^{2}-36)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the quotient rule to find ${F}^{″}(s).$

Therefore, by the smoothness property,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(-6t)}={F}^{″}(s)=-\frac{36{s}^{2}+432}{({s}^{2}-36)^{3}},\,s>6.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0 \\ L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity properties, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{-3t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =L{-3t}+L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =-3L{t}+L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that 

$$
L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}},\,s>0 \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =-3L{t}+L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =-3\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{s\cdot {s}^{2}-3({s}^{2}+1)}{{s}^{2}({s}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{{s}^{3}-3{s}^{2}-3}{{s}^{2}({s}^{2}+1)},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity properties, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{3-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t} \\  & =L{3}-L{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t} \\  & =3L{1}-L{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that 

$$
L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{1} & =\frac{1}{s},\,s>0 \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =3L{1}-L{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t} \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9} \\  & =\frac{3({s}^{2}+9)-{s}^{2}}{s({s}^{2}+9)} \\  & =\frac{3{s}^{2}+27-{s}^{2}}{s({s}^{2}+9)} \\  & =\frac{2{s}^{2}+27}{s({s}^{2}+9)},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, we expand:

$$
f(t)=(1-5t)^{2}=1-10t+25{t}^{2}
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity properties, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{1-10t+25{t}^{2}} \\  & =L{1}+L{-10t}+L{25{t}^{2}} \\  & =L{1}-10L{t}+25L{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.$ Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{1} & =\frac{1}{s},\,s>0 \\ L{t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}},\,s>0 \\ L{{t}^{2}} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{1}-10L{t}+25L{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s}-10\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+25\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s}-\frac{10}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{50}{{s}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{s}^{2}-10s+50}{{s}^{3}},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, we expand:

$$
f(t)=(4t+1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}+8t+1
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity properties, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{16{t}^{2}+8t+1} \\  & =L{16{t}^{2}}+L{8t}+L{1} \\  & =16L{{t}^{2}}+8L{t}+L{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.$ Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{2}} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}},\,s>0 \\ L{t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}},\,s>0 \\ L{1} & =\frac{1}{s},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =16L{{t}^{2}}+8L{t}+L{1} \\  & =16\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+8\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{32}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{8}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{{s}^{2}+8s+32}{{s}^{3}},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity properties, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{3}-4t+5} & =L{{t}^{3}}+L{-4t}+L{5} \\  & =L{{t}^{3}}-4L{t}+5L{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.$ Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{1} & =\frac{1}{s},\,s>0 \\ L{t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}},\,s>0 \\ L{{t}^{3}} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{t}^{3}}-4L{t}+5L{1} \\  & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}-4\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+5\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}-\frac{4}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{5}{s} \\  & =\frac{5{s}^{3}-4{s}^{2}+6}{{s}^{4}},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for every real $s>a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence. 

The smoothness property states that, for each integer $n\ge 0$ and $s>a,$ we have

$$
{F}^{(n)}(s)=(-1)^{n}\,L{{t}^{n}f(t)}.
$$

We're asked to prove the smoothness property in the case $n=2.$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L2}.$ From line $\text{L1}$ we know that

$$
F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt.
$$

By $\text{the definition of the second derivative with respect to }s$, we get

$$
{F}^{″}(s)=\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{s}^{2}}F(s)=\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{s}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt,
$$

which is exactly the statement in line $\text{L2}.$

- Next we consider line $\text{L3}.$ From $\text{L2}$ we have

$$
{F}^{″}(s)=\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{s}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt.
$$

Since $f$ is of exponential order, the integral converges, and we can
differentiate under the integral sign:

$$
{F}^{″}(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{s}^{2}}({e}^{-st}f(t))\,dt.
$$

Therefore, line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ and $\text{differentiating under the integral sign}.$

- We now consider line $\text{L5}.$ From line $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
{F}^{″}(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{s}^{2}}({e}^{-st}f(t))\,dt.
$$

Line $\text{L4}$ tells us that

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{s}^{2}}({e}^{-st}f(t))={t}^{2}{e}^{-st}f(t).
$$

Substituting this expression into the integrand in line $\text{L3}$ gives

$$
{F}^{″}(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{2}{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt.
$$

Therefore, line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{substitution}.$

questions.problem:
Let $f(t)$ be a piecewise continuous function on $[0,\infty )$ with exponential order $a,$ and consider its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)},\,s>a.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- If $f(t)$ is of exponential order $a,$ then the integral ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt$ converges for every $s>a.$
- If $f(t)$ is of exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform $F(s)$ exists for all $s>a.$
- The Laplace transform of any piecewise continuous function of exponential order is infinitely differentiable in its region of convergence.
questions.worked_solution:
If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for every real $s>a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence.

The smoothness property states that, for each integer $n\ge 0$ and every $s>a,$

$$
{F}^{(n)}(s)=(-1)^{n}\,L{{t}^{n}f(t)}.
$$

Let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Since $f$ is of exponential order and is piecewise continuous, there exist constants $K,T>0$ and $a$ such that

$$
|f(t)|\le K{e}^{at},\,t>T.
$$

When computing the Laplace transform, we multiply $f(t)$ by ${e}^{-st}.$ If $s>a$, then for all sufficiently large $t$,

$$
|{e}^{-st}f(t)|\le K{e}^{-(s-a)t}.
$$

Because $s-a>0$, the function ${e}^{-(s-a)t}$ is integrable on $[T,\infty )$, and
$f$ is bounded on $[0,T].$
Therefore, the entire integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt
$$

converges.

- Statement II is true. The standard existence theorem for the Laplace transform says that if $f$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and of exponential order $a,$ then the improper integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt
$$

converges for every $s>a.$ This is exactly what it means for $F(s)$ to exist for all $s>a.$

- Statement III is true. The smoothness theorem guarantees

$$
{F}^{(n)}(s)=(-1)^{n}\,L{{t}^{n}f(t)}
$$

for every $n\ge 0$ and each $s>a,$ which shows that $F(s)$ is infinitely differentiable, even if $f(t)$ itself is not.

Therefore, the answer is "I, II, and III."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms Using the Smoothness Property (1st Derivative)
canonical_examples.problem:
Use the smoothness property to find the Laplace transform of

$$
\mathcal L\{t \cos 5t\}.
$$

 
You may make use of the following result:

$$
\mathcal L \{\cos \omega t\} = \dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}, \qquad s > 0.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s) = \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}
$$

exists for every real $s > a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence. Moreover, for each integer $n\geq 0$ and every such $s,$ we have

$$
\mathcal{L}\{ t^n f(t) \} = (-1)^n F^{(n)}(s).
$$

In particular, for $n=1,$ we have

$$
\mathcal{L}\{ tf(t) \} = -F'(s).
$$

We have that $f(t) = \cos 5t.$ Using the given result with $\omega = 5,$ the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is 

$$
F(s) = \dfrac{s}{s^2+25},
\qquad s > 0.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $s,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+25}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(s({s}^{2}+25)^{-1}) \\  & =({s}^{2}+25)^{-1}+s(-({s}^{2}+25)^{-2}\cdot 2s) \\  & =\frac{{s}^{2}+25}{({s}^{2}+25)^{2}}-\frac{2{s}^{2}}{({s}^{2}+25)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{25-{s}^{2}}{({s}^{2}+25)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the smoothness property,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡5t}=-{F}^{′}(s)=\frac{{s}^{2}-25}{({s}^{2}+25)^{2}},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms Using the Smoothness Property (2nd Derivative)
canonical_examples.problem:
Use the smoothness property to find the Laplace transform of

$$
\mathcal L\{t^2 \sinh{5t}\}.
$$

You may make use of the following result:

$$
\mathcal L \{\sinh \omega t\} = \dfrac{\omega}{s^2-\omega^2}, \qquad s > \omega.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s) = \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}
$$

exists for every real $s > a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence. Moreover, for each integer $n\geq 0$ and every such $s,$ we have

$$
\mathcal{L}\{ t^n f(t) \} = (-1)^n F^{(n)}(s).
$$

In particular, for $n=2,$ we have

$$
\mathcal{L}\{ t^2 f(t) \} = F''(s).
$$

We have that $f(t) = \sinh 5t.$ Using the given result with $\omega = 5,$ the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is 

$$
F(s) = \dfrac{5}{s^2-25},
\qquad s > 5.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $s,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{5}{{s}^{2}-25}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(5({s}^{2}-25)^{-1}) \\  & =-5({s}^{2}-25)^{-2}\cdot 2s \\  & =-\frac{10s}{({s}^{2}-25)^{2}} \\ {F}^{″}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\frac{10s}{({s}^{2}-25)^{2}}) \\  & =-10\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{s}{({s}^{2}-25)^{2}}) \\  & =-10\cdot (\frac{(s)^{′}\cdot ({s}^{2}-25)^{2}-s\cdot {(({s}^{2}-25)^{2})}^{′}}{({s}^{2}-25)^{4}}) \\  & =-10\cdot (\frac{({s}^{2}-25)^{2}-s\cdot 2({s}^{2}-25)\cdot 2s}{({s}^{2}-25)^{4}}) \\  & =-10\cdot (\frac{({s}^{2}-25)^{2}-4{s}^{2}({s}^{2}-25)}{({s}^{2}-25)^{4}}) \\  & =-10\cdot (\frac{{s}^{2}-25-4{s}^{2}}{({s}^{2}-25)^{3}}) \\  & =-10\cdot (\frac{-3{s}^{2}-25}{({s}^{2}-25)^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{30{s}^{2}+250}{({s}^{2}-25)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the quotient rule to find $F''(s).$

Therefore, by the smoothness property,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡5t}={F}^{″}(s)=\frac{30{s}^{2}+250}{({s}^{2}-25)^{3}},\,s>5.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $\mathcal L\left\{t^n\right\} = \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}},$ find the Laplace transform of $f(t) = (t - 5)^2$ for $s > 0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
\mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\}
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants.

First, we expand:

$$
f(t) = (t - 5)^2= t^2 - 10t + 25
$$

Now, taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity properties, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{t}^{2}-10t+25} \\  & =L{{t}^{2}}+L{-10t}+L{25} \\  & =L{{t}^{2}}-10L{t}+25L{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\mathcal L\left\{t^n\right\} = \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}.$ Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{2}} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}},\,s>0 \\ L{t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}},\,s>0 \\ L{1} & =\frac{1}{s},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{t}^{2}}-10L{t}+25L{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}-10\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+25\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}-\frac{10}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{25}{s} \\  & =\frac{2-10s+25{s}^{2}}{{s}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{25{s}^{2}-10s+2}{{s}^{3}},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and its Laplace transform

$$
F(s) = \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}
$$

exists for $s > a.$ Then, $F(s)$ is twice differentiable at every point $s > a,$ and we have

$$
F''(s) = \mathcal{L}\{ t^2\cdot f(t) \}.
$$

A proof of this statement is given below. 

$\textrm{L1}{:}\:$ $F(s) = \displaystyle \int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t)\,\textrm{d}t$ exists for $s > a.$

$\textrm{L2}{:}\:$ $F''(s) = \displaystyle \frac{\textrm{d}^2}{\textrm{d}s^2}\int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t)\,\textrm{d}t$

$\textrm{L3}{:}\:$ $F''(s) = \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \frac{\partial^2}{\partial s^2}\big(e^{-st} f(t)\big)\,\textrm{d}t$

$\textrm{L4}{:}\:$ $\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2}{\partial s^2}\big(e^{-st} f(t)\big) = t^2 e^{-st} f(t)$

$\textrm{L5}{:}\:$ $F''(s) = \displaystyle \int_0^\infty t^2 e^{-st} f(t)\,\textrm{d}t$

$\textrm{L6}{:}\:$ $F''(s) = \mathcal{L}\{t^2\cdot f(t)\}$

Explain the reasoning behind:

- How line $\textrm{L2}$ follows from line $\textrm{L1}.$

- How line $\textrm{L4}$ follows from its preceding line.

- How line $\textrm{L6}$ follows from $\textrm{L5}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s) = \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}
$$

exists for every real $s > a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence. 

The smoothness property states that, for each integer $n\geq 0$ and $s > a,$ we have

$$
F^{(n)}(s) = (-1)^n\, \mathcal{L}\{ t^n f(t) \}.
$$

We're asked to prove the smoothness property in the case $n = 2.$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\textrm{L2}.$ From line $\textrm{L1}$ we know that

$$
F(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

By the definition of the second derivative with respect to $s,$ we get

$$
F''(s) = \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}s^2} F(s) = \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}s^2}\int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t,
$$

which is exactly the statement in line $\textrm{L2}.$

- We now consider line $\textrm{L4}.$ The function $f(t)$ does not depend on $s$, so

$$
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial s^2}\big(e^{-st} f(t)\big)
  = f(t)\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial s^2}(e^{-st})
  = f(t)\,\frac{\partial}{\partial s}(-te^{-st})
  = f(t)\,(t^2 e^{-st})
  = t^2 e^{-st} f(t).
$$

Thus line $\textrm{L4}$ follows from the chain rule.

- Finally, we consider line $\textrm{L6}.$ By the definition of the Laplace transform,

$$
\mathcal{L}\{t^2\cdot f(t)\}
  = \int_0^\infty e^{-st} \big(t^2 f(t)\big)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Comparing this with the integral in line $\textrm{L5}$, we see that

$$
F''(s)
  = \int_0^\infty t^2 e^{-st} f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
  = \int_0^\infty e^{-st} \big(t^2 f(t)\big)\,\mathrm{d}t
  = \mathcal{L}\{t^2\cdot f(t)\},
$$

which is exactly the expression in line $\textrm{L6}.$
